title: bluebird
text: My mom said bluebirds are a sign, a promise, that good things are ahead. As a kid, when they landed on the balcony of our cramped birthday-balloon-popping-popcorn-ceilinged 1 bedroom apartment, we would look out at them together, silent, unmoving, to not scare hope away.

When I first arrived at UC Santa Cruz, recently-fledged hope danced around the scant bushes surrounding OPERS with such regularity that I, with regularity, began to doubt that capital-G God had commandeered them from their daily goings just for me to glimpse them.

During my third year, I took Electronic Sound Synthesis III, where we each composed a soundscape and shared it with the class. One of my classmates, after sharing his composition and fielding comments, seemed to like my interpretation of his composition: that it mirrored John Coltrane's anti-colonial interpretation of the naively beautiful "My Favorite Things". Originally from Rogers & Hammerstein's "The Sound of Music", a movie which already complicates with age, "My Favorite Things" is further complicated in John Coltrane's 13 minute, 44 second, relentless, hypnotic, and haunting rendition of the piece. My classmate's worst nightmare was becoming a cog in the system, and a comparison to Coltrane's wordless critique of America's coziness with colonialism gave him hope that his creativity could escape the prison walls closing in on him. Nothing burgers made of the default piano patch and AI drummer in Logic can still channel how hope bifurcates our stories into both the cozy and the colonial, I suppose.

At the dinner table, when Coltrane's rendition came on, my mom would always skip it before the 5th time through the changes. Perhaps she felt I was not ready for how painfully complex yet persistent hope must become as one grows up. Coltrane knew. Bluebirds know. And they taught me when I was ready.

Bluebirds are statistically more common in Santa Cruz's mild Mediterranean climate, yes, but they're also placed for me, individually and intentionally, because capital-G God knows I need them to reject the all-too simple hope of heaven versus hell, and to discover that, in this very lifetime, complex hope can fuel a life proudly orthogonal to a fear of loss.
So, a few of my favorite things: Bluebirds, hope, and John Coltrane - all hail complexity.
